title: Chain of Responsibility pattern
idea: The Chain of Responsibility pattern passes a request along linked handlers until one handles it, so the sender never chooses the receiver.

analogy.text: A customer email reaches a help bot first, then an agent, then a team lead. Each one answers it or passes it up.
analogy.breaks: People can share a case; one handler owns the whole answer.

points: Each handler either handles the request or forwards it to its `next` link.
The sender knows only the first handler; a new rule is one new class.
Servlet `Filter` chains are a variant: each link may act, then pass on.
Skip it for one fixed rule; always define what happens when nobody handles.

steps.caption: The caller hands refund R-3 to the head of the chain. It never sees the other links.
`FraudCheck` finds no flag and returns empty, so `handle` forwards to `next`.
320 is over the auto limit of 50. This link passes it on too.
The agent limit is 500, so this link answers. The walk stops; finance never runs.
Flagged R-2 asks for only 40, but it stops at the first link. Order is policy.
R-4 for 9000 passes every link. The last one has no `next`.
The fallback rejects it with a reason, instead of returning nothing.

code.title: The problem: one if-chain
code.caption: Every approval rule sits in one method, in one fixed order, and the order hides a bug.

walk.text: One method holds every rule and knows every approver by name.
The small-amount branch returns first, so flagged R-2 is approved instead of held.
Limits are welded into `else if` order. You cannot reorder, reuse or test one alone.
The fallback is a bare string with no reason, added as an afterthought.
Each new rule edits this method again, against the Open/Closed Principle (OCP).

code.title: The fix: a handler chain
code.caption: Small handlers, linked once at startup; each one decides or passes the refund on.

walk.text: The chain is built in one place. Reading it top-down shows the policy order.
The request is an immutable record, validated once, so no handler can alter it.
`link` wires each handler to the next and rejects a null at build time.
`handle` is final: answer, else forward, else fall back. No subclass can skip forwarding.
Subclasses answer one question: can I handle this? Empty means pass it on.
One configurable approver replaces three near-identical classes; the limit is data.

pitfalls: Putting a cheap approver before `FraudCheck` lets flagged refunds through; order is policy, so test it.
No fallback at the end makes unhandled requests vanish silently; return a reason or throw.
A link pointing back to an earlier one loops on unhandled requests until `StackOverflowError`.

quiz.q: Same classes as the demo. What does this print?
quiz.why: `auto` is the head and 40 is within its limit, so it answers and the walk stops. `FraudCheck` never sees the flagged refund.

takeaway: Each handler handles or forwards; the chain's order is the policy.

starters: How is Chain of Responsibility different from the Decorator pattern?
Should a handler stop the chain or let every handler run, like servlet filters?
How would I make the chain order configurable without editing code?
